newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Capill sets harder NZ Christian line on coalitions.
newsitem.headline: Capill sets harder NZ Christian line on coalitions.

text.p: New Zealand Christian Coalition co-leader Graham Capill on Thursday toughened the two party grouping's position on forming a coalition after the October 12 election, saying concessions on issues such as abortion law would be a prerequisite.

Capill, the leader of the fundamentalist Christian Heritage party, said in a radio interview: "The only way we would contemplate a coalition is to see some movement on the things we believe are desperately needed in this nation.

"We would want to see the conditions (on abortion) tightened so it is applied the way it was intended. One would expect that there has to be some movement on these issues, otherwise what is the purpose of going into a coalition?
"We are not going into a coalition just to get a seat at the Cabinet table and feather our own nests."

In an interview with Reuters in August, co-leader Graeme Lee of the Christian Democrats said on issues such as abortion the Christians would not try to leverage concessions out of bigger parties, and such issues would remain conscience votes in parliament.
Lee told Reuters on Thursday the matter was "a non-issue" that eight journalists had approached him about, but he would not comment until he had seen exactly what Capill had said.

The Christian Coalition's policies on abortion, AIDS research funding, family planning and homosexuality have raised concerns among liberals in the ruling National Party over the concessions that may be required to forge a coalition.
The Christian Coalition is seen as a logical partner for National, and on current polling its backing would be crucial to National's hopes of staying in government.
Health Minister Jenny Shipley said matters such as abortion law were conscience issues that would be decided after the election.

"I would want to consider it much more carefully if it were then to be a matter of government policy and I would be very surprised if the Christian Coalition wanted to argue it as a fixed position," she said in a radio interview.
Shipley said she could not vote, as a matter of conscience, for any measure that would prevent women from getting safe, legal abortions in New Zealand.
